claim: The study used reciprocal F1 hybrids from two heterozygous mouse strains, C57BL/6 (B6) and Castaneus (CAST).
source: We obtained reciprocal F1 hybrids from two heterozygous mouse strains, C57BL/6 (B6) and Castaneus (CAST) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the experimental design.

claim: Mice were harvested in the morning of postnatal day 22–25 from seven independent crosses (3 x C57BL/6 x CAST and 4 x CAST x C57BL/6; all males).
source: Mice were harvested in the morning of postnatal day 22–25 from seven independent crosses (3 x C57BL/6 x CAST and 4 x CAST x C57BL/6; all males).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental subjects.

claim: The study obtained 376 million uniquely mapped ChRO-seq reads across all eight organs.
source: We obtained 376 million uniquely mapped ChRO-seq reads across all eight organs (21–86 million reads per organ; Supplementary file 1) after sequencing, filtering, and mapping short reads to individual B6 and CAST genomes.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript describing the sequencing results.

claim: Hierarchical clustering using Spearman's rank correlation of ChRO-seq reads in GENCODE annotated gene bodies grouped samples from the same organ.
source: Hierarchical clustering using Spearman's rank correlation of ChRO-seq reads in GENCODE annotated gene bodies (v.M25) grouped samples from the same organ (Figure 1B), as expected based on studies comparing multiple organs across different species (Gilad and Mizrahi-Man, 2015; Merkin et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 1B showing clustering results, with citations to prior studies.

claim: Organs with similarities in organ function clustered together, for instance: heart and skeletal muscle, and large intestine and stomach.
source: Additionally, organs with similarities in organ function clustered together, for instance: heart and skeletal muscle, and large intestine and stomach (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 1B showing clustering patterns.

claim: 1374 genes and lincRNAs showed significantly higher transcription on either the B6 or CAST allele in at least one organ, comprising about 8% of the 17,703 annotated genes.
source: We identified 1374 genes and lincRNAs with strong evidence that transcription was significantly higher across the gene body on either the B6 or CAST allele in at least one organ, comprising about 8% of the 17,703 annotated genes.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript describing the analysis results.

claim: Most allelic changes were specific to a single organ.
source: Visualizing the pattern of allelic transcription revealed that most allelic changes were specific to a single organ (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 1C showing organ-specific patterns.

claim: A minority of annotated genes showed evidence of genomic imprinting (n=51), and these were generally imprinted in all organs analyzed.
source: A minority of annotated genes showed evidence of genomic imprinting (n=51), and these were generally imprinted in all organs analyzed here (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in text with specific number and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The imprinted domain associated with Angelman syndrome contained twenty ncRNAs and four genes that were transcribed more highly from the paternal allele and two genes transcribed from the maternal allele.
source: For instance, the imprinted domain associated with Angelman syndrome contained twenty ncRNAs and four genes that were transcribed more highly from the paternal allele and two genes transcribed from the maternal allele (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in text with specific counts and supported by Figure 1D showing the genomic region.

claim: Genes with allelic bias were significantly more likely to have allelic changes in the expression of an adjacent transcript compared with genes which were not changed (brain: p-value = 5.35e-4, liver: p-value < 2.2e-16; Fisher's Exact Test).
source: Indeed, we found that genes with allelic bias were significantly more likely to have allelic changes in the expression of an adjacent transcript compared with genes which were not changed (brain: p-value = 5.35e-4, liver: p-value < 2.2e-16; Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: Stated in text with specific statistical test results.

claim: The study identified 3494 domains that showed consistent evidence of allelic imbalance using AlleleHMM.
source: We identified 3494 domains that showed consistent evidence of allelic imbalance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Stated in text with specific number and reference to supplementary materials.

claim: The majority of domains (n=3466) had consistent effects in each mouse strain (called strain-effect domains).
source: The majority of these domains (n=3466) had consistent effects in each mouse strain (called strain-effect domains), the pattern expected if allelic imbalance was caused by DNA sequence differences between strains.
evidence: Stated in text with specific number and interpretation.

claim: Twenty-eight domains showed consistent evidence of genomic imprinting (imprinted domains).
source: Twenty-eight domains showed consistent evidence of genomic imprinting (imprinted domains).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript with specific number.

claim: Both strain-effect and imprinted domains spanned broad genomic regions (~10–1000 kb; Figure 1E) that were frequently composed of two or more transcription units.
source: On average, both strain-effect and imprinted domains spanned broad genomic regions (~10–1000 kb; Figure 1E) that were frequently composed of two or more transcription units, including annotated genes and ncRNAs (either long intergenic ncRNAs and/ or enhancer-templated RNAs; Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated in text with size range and supported by Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: Imprinted domains tended to be larger, have allelic differences detected across multiple tissues, and affected larger numbers of genes than strain effect domains.
source: Imprinted domains tended to be larger, have allelic differences detected across multiple tissues, and affected larger numbers of genes than strain effect domains (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figures 1E and 1F showing comparisons.

claim: The 5' end of nascent RNA, denoted by the 5' end of paired-end ChRO-seq reads, marks the transcription start site (TSS) of that nascent RNA.
source: The 5' end of nascent RNA, denoted by the 5' end of paired-end ChRO-seq reads, marks the transcription start site (TSS) of that nascent RNA (Kwak et al., 2013; Tome et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to prior work establishing this method.

claim: Most organs, especially brain and liver, had high information content showing the initiator element at maxTSSs.
source: Most organs, especially brain and liver (which were the most deeply sequenced and are the focus of the analysis below unless otherwise specified), had high information content showing the initiator element at maxTSSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A showing sequence logos.

claim: Allelic changes in TSSs were common, occurring in ~16–34% of TSCs tagged with SNPs (n=1,109–5,793; binomial test FDR <0.1).
source: Allelic changes in TSSs were common, occurring in ~16–34% of TSCs tagged with SNPs (n=1,109–5,793; binomial test FDR <0.1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentages, counts, and statistical criteria.

claim: Changes in TSSs were highly enriched within strain effect domains identified by AlleleHMM (odds ratios 3.5–5.4; p<2.2e-16, Fisher's exact test).
source: Changes in TSSs were highly enriched within strain effect domains identified by AlleleHMM (Chou and Danko, 2019) (odds ratios 3.5–5.4; p<2.2e-16, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Stated in text with specific statistical results and citation.

claim: CA initiators which changed to TA had the lowest magnitude of change in ChRO-seq signal, whereas CA dinucleotides that changed to CG had the largest magnitude of change in signal.
source: CA initiators which changed to TA had the lowest magnitude of change in ChRO-seq signal, whereas CA dinucleotides that changed to CG had the largest magnitude of change in signal.
evidence: Stated in text describing the analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The results suggest a hierarchy of initiation frequency, in which Pol II prefers to initiate at a CA dinucleotide, followed by TA, TG, and finally CG.
source: Our results suggest a hierarchy of initiation frequency, in which Pol II prefers to initiate at a CA dinucleotide, followed by TA, TG, and finally CG.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: This hierarchy observed in mammals differs substantially from yeast, which favors CG over either TA or TG.
source: This hierarchy observed in mammals differs substantially from yeast, which favors CG over either TA or TG (Zhu et al., 2021), but is more closely aligned with the importance of A in mammals based on promoter mutagenesis studies (Javahery et al., 1994; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017; Smale and Kadonaga, 2003).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to prior work in yeast and mammals.

claim: The study identified 1006 (brain) and 1389 (liver) TSCs in which the shape of the 5' end of mapped reads within that TSC changed between alleles (FDR ≤ 0.1; Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test).
source: Our approach identified 1006 (brain) and 1389 (liver) TSCs in which the shape of the 5' end of mapped reads within that TSC changed between alleles (FDR ≤ 0.1; Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test) (see examples in Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and statistical criteria, with examples in figures.

claim: Only ~10–20% of the TSCs with shape changes were also found inside of strain effect domains, indicating that these changes in shape were fundamentally different from changes in initiation rates.
source: We note that changes in the shape of signal within TSCs may not always alter the total abundance of Pol II, as compensatory changes in the rates of Pol II initiation at nearby TSSs may compensate for one another. Consistent with this hypothesis, only ~10–20% of the TSCs identified using this approach were also found inside of strain effect domains, indicating that these changes in shape were fundamentally different from changes in initiation rates and reflected a different underlying biological process.
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentages and interpretation.

claim: Single position driven allele-specific TSCs were associated with a strong, focal enrichment of SNPs around the max TSS.
source: Single position driven allele-specific TSCs were associated with a strong, focal enrichment of SNPs around the max TSS (Figure 3C [liver] and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B [brain]).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by figures showing SNP enrichment patterns.

claim: SNPs within 5 bp of the initiation site explain up to ~15%–20% of single-base driven allele-specific TSCs.
source: SNPs within 5 bp of the initiation site explain up to ~15%–20% of single-base driven allele-specific TSCs (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentages and supported by figures.

claim: The A in the initiation site may be the most important genetic determinant of transcription initiation.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the A in the initiation site may be the most important genetic determinant of transcription initiation, consistent with the Pol II initiation preference analysis conducted above (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the data with reference to prior analysis.

claim: Multiple position driven allele-specific TSCs had a weaker, broader enrichment of SNPs.
source: Multiple position driven allele-specific TSCs had a weaker, broader enrichment of SNPs (Figure 3E [liver] and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D [brain], yellow shade indicates FDR ≤ 0.05; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by figures showing SNP enrichment patterns.

claim: A higher frequency of A and T alleles downstream of the initiator motif on the allele with a higher max TSS was observed.
source: Next, we examined other factors near the TSC, aside from DNA within the initiator motif or other known PIC components, that contributed to the position of TSSs. We noticed a higher frequency of A and T alleles downstream of the initiator motif on the allele with a higher max TSS (Figure 3D).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 3D showing base composition differences.

claim: A significantly higher AT content on the allele with the highest max TSS was identified after masking DNA at positions –1 and 0.
source: Indeed, a more direct examination of AT content in 5 bp windows near the maxTSS identified a significantly higher AT content on the allele with the highest max TSS after masking DNA at positions –1 and 0 to avoid confounding effects of the initiator element (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in text with specific methodology and supported by figures.

claim: Multiple aspects of DNA sequence, including both sequence motif composition (especially the initiator element) and the energetics of DNA melting, influence TSS choice in mammalian cells.
source: We conclude that multiple aspects of DNA sequence, including both sequence motif composition (especially the initiator element) and the energetics of DNA melting, influence TSS choice in mammalian cells.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the analyses presented.

claim: Candidate initiator motifs within 20 bp of the CA/ non-CA initiation site had slightly more initiation signal on the non-CA allele compared with the CA allele.
source: Candidate initiator motifs within 20 bp of the CA/ non-CA initiation site had slightly more initiation signal on the non-CA allele compared with the CA allele, consistent with the shooting gallery model but inconsistent with the prevailing model of independent TSSs expected in mammals (Figure 4B; purple).
evidence: Stated in text with interpretation and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Higher initiation signals on the non-CA allele were observed both upstream and downstream of the initiator dinucleotide.
source: Unexpectedly, we also observed consistently higher initiation signals on the non-CA allele both upstream and downstream of the initiator dinucleotide (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 4C showing the distribution.

claim: The signal for an increase on the non-CA allele stretched up to 20 bp both upstream and downstream of the CA/ non-CA dinucleotide.
source: The signal for an increase on the non-CA allele stretched up to 20 bp both upstream and downstream of the CA/ non-CA dinucleotide.
evidence: Stated in text describing the extent of the observed effect.

claim: After DNA melting and Pol II assembly on the template strand, Pol II rapidly and stochastically moves in both directions along the template strand scanning for an energetically favorable initiator dinucleotide in a process resembling Brownian motion.
source: Instead, we propose that after DNA melting and Pol II assembly on the template strand, Pol II rapidly and stochastically moves in both directions along the template strand scanning for an energetically favorable initiator dinucleotide in a process resembling Brownian motion (Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated as a proposed model based on the data, with illustration in Figure 4E.

claim: The increased initiation signal was limited to within ~20 bp of the CA/ non-CA initiation site.
source: We found that the increased initiation signal was limited to within ~20 bp of the CA/ non-CA initiation site (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 4F showing the spatial constraint.

claim: The study identified 2260 dREG sites with candidate changes in the shape of paused Pol II (FDR ≤ 0.1; Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test).
source: Our analysis identified 2260 dREG sites with candidate changes in the shape of paused Pol II, assessed using the position of the Pol II active site, defined as the 3' end of RNA insert (FDR ≤ 0.1; Kolmogorov-Smirnov [KS] test; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in text with specific number and statistical criteria.

claim: Allelic changes in the position of paused Pol II were often coincident with changes in transcription initiation, particularly when the changes were large.
source: Previous work has shown a tight correspondence between the site of transcription initiation and pausing, with pausing occurring predominantly in the window 20–60 bp downstream of the TSS (Tome et al., 2018). As expected, allelic changes in the position of paused Pol II were often coincident with changes in transcription initiation (Figure 5A), particularly when the changes were large.
evidence: Stated in text with citation to prior work and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: In at least 111 cases (~31% of 359 total sites tagged by a SNP), the position of the max pause was identical between alleles, but the position of the max TSS changed by 1–32 bp.
source: In at least 111 cases (~31% of 359 total sites tagged by a SNP), the position of the max pause was identical between alleles, but the position of the max TSS changed by 1–32 bp (Figure 5B, top).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: 575 cases (~69% of 823 total sites tagged by a SNP) were identified in which the Pol II pause position changed while both alleles shared the same max TSS.
source: Conversely, we identified 575 cases (~69% of 823 total sites tagged by a SNP) in which the Pol II pause position changed while both alleles shared the same max TSS (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Changes in pause position were enriched for small insertions and deletions between the maxTSS and pause site (n=56 (21%); expected = 22 (8%); p<1e-5, Fisher's exact test).
source: In our dataset, changes in pausing were highly enriched for small insertions and deletions between the maxTSS and pause site (n=56 (21%); expected = 22 (8%); p<1e-5, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers and statistical test results.

claim: Changes in pause position were correlated with changes in the size of the insertion or deletion, such that the number of bases between the max TSS and the pause was typically less than 5 bp.
source: Changes in pause position were correlated with changes in the size of the insertion or deletion, such that the number of bases between the max TSS and the pause was typically less than 5 bp (Figure 5C).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 5C showing the correlation.

claim: Pol II pauses on the C position immediately after a G-rich stretch.
source: Thus, our data show that Pol II pauses on the C position immediately after a G-rich stretch.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the sequence analysis presented.

claim: Allelic differences at the RNA polymerase active site (usually a C) had the strongest association with the pause, followed by SNPs at the –2 and –3 position relative to the pause (usually a G).
source: Allelic differences at the RNA polymerase active site (usually a C) had the strongest association with the pause, followed by SNPs at the –2 and –3 position relative to the pause (usually a G; Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by figures showing SNP enrichment patterns.

claim: Indels and SNPs explained 49% of allele-specific differences in the pause position.
source: Collectively, indels and SNPs identified as enriched in the analysis above explained 49% of allele-specific differences in the pause position (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentage and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: DNA sequence changes affecting pause position occurred at the short pause position on the long allele.
source: We found that the DNA sequence motif near the long pause position was similar on both alleles, recapitulating the C at the pause site and an enrichment of Gs in the transcription bubble (Figure 5G, right). By contrast, DNA sequence changes affecting pause position occurred at the short pause position on the long allele (Figure 5G; bottom left).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 5G showing sequence logos.

claim: When there was a SNP in the active site at the short pause, the max pause position moved downstream by <10 bp.
source: In favor of this model, when there was a SNP in the active site at the short pause, the max pause position moved downstream by <10 bp, a relatively small amount compared to all changes in pause shape (Figure 5H).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 5H showing the distribution.

claim: Indels between the initiation and short pause site tended to have a larger effect on the allelic difference between pause positions.
source: By contrast, indels between the initiation and short pause site tended to have a larger effect on the allelic difference between pause positions (Figure 5I).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 5I showing the distribution.

claim: The study identified 317–931 candidate allelic termination windows in each of the eight organs (total n=3,450).
source: We identified 317–931 candidate allelic termination windows in each of the eight organs (total n=3,450).
evidence: Stated in text with specific numbers for each organ and total.

claim: Allelic termination windows varied in size between 1 kb and 100 kb, with a median size just under 10 kb.
source: Allelic termination windows varied in size between 1 kb and 100 kb, with a median size just under 10 kb (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in text with size range and median, supported by figures.

claim: Allelic termination windows were more likely to have allelic changes in the transcription level of an adjacent transcript compared with matched transcripts without an allelic termination window (liver: odds ratio = 1.65, p=1.83e-15; brain: odds ratio = 1.23, p=0.018; Fisher's exact test).
source: Additionally, allelic termination windows were more likely to have allelic changes in the transcription level of an adjacent transcript compared with matched transcripts without an allelic termination window (liver: odds ratio = 1.65, p=1.83e-15; brain: odds ratio = 1.23, p=0.018; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Stated in text with specific statistical results.

claim: The expression of nearby transcription units was frequently highest on the allele that terminated early (liver: odds ratio = 4.97, p=2.2e-16; brain: odds ratio = 9.67, p=2.2e-16; Fisher's exact test).
source: Intriguingly, the expression of nearby transcription units was frequently highest on the allele that terminated early (liver: odds ratio = 4.97, p=2.2e-16; brain: odds ratio = 9.67, p=2.2e-16; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Stated in text with specific statistical results.

claim: 21–41% of transcription units with differences in allelic termination had evidence of changes in mRNA primary structure identified using AlleleHMM.
source: Our analysis determined that 21–41% of transcription units with differences in allelic termination had evidence of changes in mRNA primary structure identified using AlleleHMM (Figure 6D), an enrichment of two- to fourfold relative to transcription units with no evidence of allelic termination (p<2.2e-16; Fisher's exact test in both brain and liver).
evidence: Stated in text with specific percentages and statistical results, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: Allelic changes in mRNA primary structure were more likely to have increased differences in mRNA stability between B6 and CAST alleles (Brain p=4.28e-4, liver p=2.69e-08; KS test).
source: Allelic changes in mRNA primary structure were more likely to have increased differences in mRNA stability between B6 and CAST alleles (Brain p=4.28e-4, liver p=2.69e-08; KS test; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-C).
evidence: Stated in text with specific statistical results and supported by figures.

claim: Pol II transcription is a cyclic process that can be divided into stages representing transcription initiation, pause, elongation, and termination.
source: Transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) results in the synthesis of mRNAs encoding all protein-coding genes. Pol II transcription is a cyclic process that can be divided into stages representing transcription initiation, pause, elongation, and termination (Fuda et al., 2009; Jonkers and Lis, 2015).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to prior work establishing this framework.

claim: Pol II pauses near the transcription start site of nearly all genes in metazoan genomes.
source: After initiation, Pol II pauses near the transcription start site of nearly all genes in metazoan genomes (Jonkers et al., 2014; Muse et al., 2007; Rougvie and Lis, 1988).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to prior work establishing this phenomenon.

claim: DNA sequence motifs such as the TATA box, B recognition element (BRE), and the initiator motif are reported to bind proteins in the PIC and thereby set the transcription start site.
source: DNA sequence motifs such as the TATA box, B recognition element (BRE), and the initiator motif are reported to bind proteins in the PIC and thereby set the transcription start site (Carninci et al., 2006; Nilson et al., 2017; Smale and Baltimore, 1989).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to prior work identifying these motifs.

claim: SNPs affecting core transcription initiation motifs can affect the rates of mRNA production.
source: SNPs affecting these core transcription initiation motifs can affect the rates of mRNA production indicating the central importance of DNA sequence affecting transcription initiation (Kristjánsdóttir et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to prior work demonstrating this effect.

claim: DNA sequence motifs involved in Pol II transcription are weak, degenerate, and spread across wide genomic regions.
source: In all cases, these studies show that DNA sequence motifs involved in Pol II transcription are weak, degenerate, and spread across wide genomic regions.
evidence: Stated as a summary of prior studies on DNA sequence motifs.

claim: The ~20 bp distance limitation observed reflects structural constraints placed on Brownian motion by the PIC or the RNA Polymerase complex.
source: It seems likely that the ~20 bp distance limitation we observed reflects structural constraints placed on Brownian motion by the PIC or the RNA Polymerase complex.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: The enrichment of G nucleotides in the transcription bubble has a higher stability of RNA-DNA hybridization without using a cytosine nucleotide, and may serve to stabilize the RNA-DNA hybrid within the transcription bubble while Pol II remains paused.
source: The enrichment of G nucleotides in the transcription bubble has a higher stability of RNA-DNA hybridization without using a cytosine nucleotide, and may serve to stabilize the RNA-DNA hybrid within the transcription bubble while Pol II remains paused.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the observed sequence patterns.

claim: Allelic differences in transcription termination were largely similar between different organs, implicating a single DNA sequence code as the major determinant of transcription termination across organs studied.
source: Allelic differences in transcription termination were largely similar between different organs, implicating a single DNA sequence code as the major determinant of transcription termination across organs studied here.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the consistency of termination patterns across organs.

claim: Novel isoforms are likely to be a minor portion of the mRNA produced from the allele with the longer transcription unit.
source: We emphasize that novel isoforms are likely to be a minor portion of the mRNA produced from the allele with the longer transcription unit, which could help explain why differences in mRNA stability occur at a relatively small portion of mRNAs with changes in primary structure.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation to explain the observed patterns in mRNA stability.

claim: The use of an F1 hybrid system reduces artifacts from larger changes in DNA sequence composition on the sequencing library itself.
source: Another advantage of using a F1 hybrid system is that by comparing the effect of SNPs or indels on otherwise very similar DNA sequences, we can reduce artifacts from larger changes in DNA sequence composition on the sequencing library itself.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the experimental design.

claim: Batch effects are shared between the B6 and CAST alleles, which are processed from the same nucleus and undergo exactly the same experimental processing and sequencing steps.
source: Experimental batch variation is a major confounder in all genomic analyses. However, batch effects are shared between the B6 and CAST alleles, which are processed from the same nucleus and undergo exactly the same experimental processing and sequencing steps.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the F1 hybrid experimental design.

claim: The dynamics of Pol II on each position of the genome can influence the rate of mRNA production and may impact organism phenotypes.
source: The dynamics of Pol II on each position of the genome can influence the rate of mRNA production and may impact organism phenotypes.
evidence: Stated as a broader implication of the study's findings.
